note:
The book of Jonah falls into two main divisions, each introduced by the sentence, “Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah.” The first division comprises two sections: the call, flight, and judgment of Jonah (ch. 1), and the thanksgiving psalm (ch. 2).

**1:1–17** This passage depicts Jonah’s disobedient response to his commission as a prophet to go to Nineveh, but it does not tell us Jonah’s reason for fleeing from God (which is not revealed until 4:2). Here we witness Jonah’s interaction with the Gentile sailors, which involves a theme prominent in the book’s second division—the Lord’s mercy to Gentiles. Despite Jonah’s disobedience and hypocrisy, the sailors do not despise Jonah’s God, but see the clear hand of the God of Israel and respond in worship. In contrast with Jonah, the Gentile sailors are careful to avoid personal sin before God (v. 14). The prophet of God is judged, but the Gentiles are spared, an event that foreshadows the response and sparing of the Ninevites in the book’s second division.

**1:1 Now the word of the** LORD **came to Jonah.** With some variations, wording like this is used some 112 times in the OT to describe the giving of a divine message to a prophet.

**Jonah the son of Amittai.** The recipient of the Lord’s revelation is Jonah (“dove”), the son of Amittai (“loyal” or “faithful”). This designation identifies the prophet as the historical character of 2 Kin. 14:25, who proclaimed that Jeroboam II (793–753 B.C.) would recover territory from the Syrians to the north. Contrast Jonah’s message to Jeroboam’s kingdom with the words of Amos and Hosea, who prophesied during the period of Israel’s spiritual decline in the latter part of the eighth century (see Introduction: Date and Occasion).

The Lord’s sovereignty over all the nations is implicit in the command to Jonah. He is the “Judge of all the earth” (Gen. 18:25). The last capital of the Assyrian Empire, Nineveh was on the east side of the Tigris River directly opposite the modern city of Mosul in northern Iraq. The site has been extensively excavated and boasts a long and rich history. It is noteworthy that Assyria exacted tribute from an earlier Israelite king named Jehu (841–814 B.C.;2 Kin. 10:34 note). So from the perspective of the book’s original audience, who lived in the eighth century B.C., Assyria is still feared in the memory of the Israelite people, even though the military threat of the Assyrians had temporarily subsided.

**call out against it.** Though it is not disclosed here, Jonah understands that his pronouncement of the Lord’s judgment on the feared and hated Assyrian Empire is reversible (4:2 note). He knows that his message offers the opportunity for repentance.

**their evil has come up before me.** In the later prophecy of Nahum (seventh century B.C.), the Assyrian capital of Nineveh is the focus of divine wrath and is depicted as the embodiment of evil and cruelty (Nah. 3:1–7). In Nahum’s day, the Assyrian war machine is guilty of horrendous atrocities. In 612 B.C., that empire would itself fall victim to a cruel destroyer.

Precise identification of this Tarshish is difficult, though it is often taken to be the mining port of Tartessus in southern Spain. Sometimes, however, the term designates distant Mediterranean coastlands in general. In either case, Jonah has fled in the opposite direction from Nineveh.

**from the presence of the ** LORD**.** Because God is present even “in the uttermost parts of the sea” (Ps. 139:9), escape is impossible.

LORD **hurled a great wind upon the sea.** Jonah’s God is creator and lord of the sea (Gen. 1:10, 21; Ex. 14:21; Mark 4:41). The ferocity of the storm is evident from the fear of these seasoned sailors and the fact that the ship is in danger of breaking up.

The casting of lots was a common form of divination in the ancient world, a device used to discover the will of the gods. This method of discerning the will of the true God was not forbidden in ancient Israel, for the Lord rules even over lots (Lev. 16:8–10; Num. 26:55; Josh. 18:6–10; Judg. 20:9; 1 Sam. 10:19–21; Neh. 10:34, 11:1; Prov. 16:33, 18:18; cf. Acts 1:24–26).

See note on Gen. 14:13. Jonah identifies himself in ethnic terms. The term “Hebrew” is commonly used by Israelites to identify themselves to foreigners (Gen. 40:15; Ex. 1:19; 3:18; 10:3).

**I fear the ** LORD**.** Jonah also identifies himself in religious terms. The word order focuses attention on the divine name. The Lord his God is not just a personal, family, or national deity. He is the supreme and sovereign God, creator of land and sea.

**the God of heaven.** An old title (Gen. 24:3, 7) also commonly used in the Persian period after the exile (2 Chr. 36:23; Ezra 1:2; Neh. 1:4, 5; 2:4).

LORD **appointed.** The same Hebrew word also occurs three times in 4:6–8. Each instance indicates a startling example of God’s sovereignty over the natural world. God’s mercy is also displayed, as Jonah is saved in spite of his stubborn disobedience.

**a great fish.** The species of whale or fish that swallows Jonah cannot be identified with certainty. Suggestions have included the sperm whale or a large shark. The fish is God’s instrument to rescue Jonah from the depths of the sea (“the belly of Sheol”; 2:2).

**three days and three nights.** Jesus referred to the book of Jonah to communicate truths regarding His own message and mission (Matt. 12:38–41; 16:4; Luke 11:29–32). He spoke of the “sign of the prophet Jonah” not only with reference to the three days and three nights that Jonah was in the fish (Matt. 12:39, 40), but also with regard to the efficacy of Jonah’s preaching. Without benefit of a miraculous sign, the Ninevites recognized Jonah’s message as one with divine authority, and they responded in repentance.

Jonah’s response to God’s judgment is framed as a thanksgiving psalm (v. 9). The cry of the prophet focuses on the desperate character of his situation by using terms typical in poetic descriptions of death or nearness to death. In his plight he looks to the Lord’s holy temple, the physical token of the Lord’s saving presence with His people. The psalm is a moving testimony to the heart of Israel’s faith and to the heart of the prophet, but he still has much to learn. His vision of God’s mercy is still too narrow at this point, as the final chapter of the book reveals.

**2:1 Jonah prayed.** Consistent with OT narrative style, the Jonah story is interrupted with a poem (vv. 2–9), a psalm of thanksgiving and celebration for the Lord’s deliverance and mercy. The literary structure is typical of a thanksgiving psalm: (1) petition for deliverance (2:2); (2) review of crisis (2:3–6); (3) review of deliverance (2:6, 7); and (4) praise for deliverance (2:8, 9).

verse_quote: I called out ... and he answered me.
note: Using the poetic device of parallelism, Jonah’s psalm is introduced in two couplets that tell of the prophet’s prayer and the Lord’s answer. Jonah acknowledges that he has been rescued “out of the belly of Sheol.” Personified in this instance as having an insatiable appetite, “Sheol” can refer either to death itself or to the realm of the dead where the wicked go.

These verses contain a vivid recollection of the near-death crisis, its causes, and its results. Jonah’s plight is the Lord’s judgment on his disobedience. The brush with a watery grave is presented with graphic imagery: entanglement in seaweed, the silence of deep water, and waves swelling high above the victim.

verse_quote: I am driven away from your sight.
note:
For the prophet, the ultimate horror of death is separation from the presence of the Lord (Ps. 88:4, 5, 10–12).

**yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.** The Jerusalem temple is the earthly location of the divine presence. Jonah longs for the communion with God that the temple affords. The prophet laments losing the same divine presence that he earlier sought to escape (1:3, 10).

Jonah was at death’s door. His slow, silent descent through the depths, like a journey to the underworld, brought him to “the gates of death” just before his rescue (Ps. 9:13).

**you brought up my life from the pit.** Here “pit” is used to describe the realm of death (Job 33:22, 24; Ps. 49:9; Is. 51:14). Despite the hopelessness of the circumstances, the repentant prophet is rescued from the realm of the dead and restored to communion with God.
LORD**.** The context indicates that this prayer is answered. The importance and effectiveness of prayer are again emphasized, as in v. 2 (cf. Heb. 4:16).

verse_quote: Those who pay regard to vain idols.
note:
Recalling the ineffectiveness of the sailors’ prayers and of their gods (1:5), Jonah condemns those who put their faith in idols.

**forsake their hope of steadfast love** . This may be an indirect reference to the Israelites. The word translated “steadfast love” is _hesed_, which often describes God’s covenant faithfulness to His people. This verse warns that those who worship idols abandon God’s _hesed_ toward them.

LORD**.** Like Joshua before him (Josh. 24:14, 15), Jonah declares his loyalty to the Lord and extols Him as the only source of salvation and deliverance. In imparting salvation to Jonah, the Lord moves the prophet from disobedience to repentance; in imparting salvation to the Ninevites, He will move them from idolatry to faith (3:5–10); in imparting salvation to the Gentiles in the new covenant era—as under the old covenant—He sovereignly moves them to faith and repentance (Acts 11:17, 18).

LORD **spoke ... it vomited Jonah.** Again creation responds obediently to the sovereign commands of the Creator (1:4, 15, 17). By grace, the fish has served as God’s instrument to deliver Jonah to safety.

In this second division of the book, Jonah preaches the message God has commanded, and the people of Nineveh respond with genuine repentance (ch. 3). When the Lord turns from threatened judgment, the real reason Jonah fled the first time is revealed in the text: he feared that God would show mercy to the hated Assyrians (4:2). In the object lessons that follow, the wideness of the Lord’s mercy and compassion is revealed (4:5–11).

Having learned that the call of God is irrevocable (cf. Rom. 11:29), Jonah responds to the Lord’s renewed commission.

**Nineveh was.** Some have suggested that the use of the past tense (“was”) indicates that the city no longer existed at the time of writing. Given the city’s destruction in 612 B.C. by the Medes and Babylonians, this interpretation would date the narrative sometime after the late seventh century B.C. The past tense does not preclude an eighth-century date, however, for it may simply indicate the status of the city when the prophet arrived.

**an exceedingly great city, three days’** **journey.** Many commentators interpret these phrases as a reference to the physical size of Nineveh. Archaeological exploration has shown that the city was between seven and eight miles in circumference. Others suggest that the first formula should be translated “a very important city,” or “a great city to God” (emphasizing its significance rather than size). The second expression (lit. “journey of three days”) could indicate the duration of visit appropriate (in terms of ancient Near Eastern diplomatic protocol) for an emissary to such an important city. Alternatively, the expression “the great city” (1:2, 3:2; 4:11) could refer to “Greater Nineveh”, a region that also included the cities of Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen (see Gen. 10:11, 12).

Jonah’s worst fears are realized (cf. v. 10; 4:1, 2) when the people believe, repent, proclaim a fast, and adorn themselves in sackcloth (the traditional mourning garb of the ancient Near East). The repentance is swift and citywide. The narrator indirectly cites this repentance on behalf of the Ninevites to indict his Israelite audience for their lack of repentance and for their lack of zeal for holiness and righteousness.

An unusual way to refer to the king of Assyria. In the light of Assyrian politics during the mid-eighth century B.C., the term “king” can be used here of a strong provincial ruler who exercises control over the region of Nineveh. During this period, the authority of the king of Assyria is somewhat limited.

**he arose ... and sat in ashes.** The king’s response is as immediate and spontaneous as that of his subjects. Royal authority gives way to penitent humility. He exchanges his robes for sackcloth and his throne for a bed of ashes (cf. Job 42:6; Is. 58:5).

With the royal edict mandating prayer, mourning rites, and a fast for man and beast, Nineveh’s repentance is complete. The inclusion of animals points to the thorough and genuine nature of their repentance. Later, it is customary among the Persians to include domestic animals in the rites of mourning.
This royal admonition addresses the most prominent of Nineveh’s sins. Physical violence and social injustice are hallmarks of the Assyrian Empire during the biblical era (Nah. 3:1).

The king gives personal and corporate expression to the hope that genuine repentance may avert the divine judgment. The structure of 3:5–9 conforms to the typical OT pattern of reporting corporate repentance (Jer. 36:3; Joel 2): (1) threat of judgment; (2) penitent response; and (3) divine decision to withhold punishment.

The prophetic warning (v. 4) had an implied condition, namely, that judgment was imminent—if the city did not repent. In turning “from their evil way” the Nine­vites have met that condition.

**God relented.** When the Bible narrates God’s actions, it often does so in anthropomorphic terms, i.e., ascribing to God human characteristics. This change in God’s actions does not imply a change in His sovereign will. The Lord’s apparent change of mind (i.e., His sovereign choice to carry out His own action in a way that is appropriate to a human response) is fully compatible with God’s sovereignty and immutability, since He ordains the means as well as the ends of His sovereign will (Jer. 18:7–10). See note on Gen. 6:6.

The book concludes with angry Jonah receiving a lesson in divine mercy and compassion from God Himself. Strikingly, the text does not explain how Jonah responds to this instruction. Instead, it ends leaving the reader with the contrast between Jonah’s resentful attitude and God’s great mercy to the Ninevites.

**4:1 it displeased Jonah exceedingly.** The Hebrew is particularly vivid (lit. “it was evil to Jonah as a great wrong”). Jonah expresses his emotion in the strongest language possible: his greatest fear before going to Nineveh was that the Lord would bestow forgiveness on Israel’s most-hated enemy (v. 2), and this forgiveness is what has occurred.

verse_quote: you are a gracious ... relenting from disaster.
note: The reason for Jonah’s initial flight to Tarshish is revealed. Despite his blatant disobedience and narrow-mindedness, Jonah understands the character of God. Here he is echoing an important statement describing God’s mercy to an undeserving Israel (e.g., Ex. 34:6; Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 103:8; Joel 2:13). Only here and in Joel 2:13 is the reference to divine repentance (“he relents over disaster”) included (3:10 note), an inclusion appropriate to the context of Nineveh’s repentance and deliverance.

verse_quote: Jonah went out ... made a booth.
note: Grateful for his own deliverance, Jonah still refuses to accept that of the Ninevites. Hoping that the Lord will execute judgment, Jonah leaves the city for a vantage point from which to view its destruction.

LORD **God appointed a plant.** See note on 1:17. Probably because of the shortage of timber in this dry region, Jonah’s shelter is not adequate to provide protection from the hot Near Eastern sun. The type of vegetation provided is uncertain. Although some suggest the castor oil plant, which grows quickly to a height of fifteen feet (4.5 m), a climbing plant, like a gourd, is more likely.

The same divine hand that in mercy provided the great fish and the shade now brings a worm to kill the plant and a hot east wind to torment the bitter prophet. Jonah struggles to understand why God acts as He does, providing protection one day and removing it the next. The episode with the plant mirrors larger events. The plant provided temporary shelter to Jonah and Nineveh’s repentance means that Israel is temporarily safe from Assyria’s violent invitation. However, just as the plant falls away and Jonah suffers, a future generation of Ninevites will, within decades, revert to the empire’s typical behavior and destroy the northern kingdom of Israel. Jonah cannot understand why God would permit this to happen. He cannot accept that God is willing pardon the people of Nineveh, who deserve to be punished for their wickedness., 8

The divine intention of the object lessons is revealed here. God’s magnificent compassion for the people and animals He creates and sustains (v. 11) is contrasted with Jonah’s petty concern for the plant (v. 10). The reader may recall Jesus’ compassion as He looked upon the multitudes (Matt. 9:36; Mark 6:34; 8:2), and His statement in Matt. 10:29 that not a sparrow will fall to the ground apart from the Father’s will. In its infancy, the largely Jewish NT church later wrestles with this issue of the wideness of God’s mercy raised here in the book of Jonah, as the Lord opens the hearts of the Gentiles to obey the gospel (Acts 11:18; 15:14; 28:28).
